chunks: And with this chain of transmission: from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Zayd al-Shahham, who said:
I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (AS) about al-khafqah and al-khafqatayn.
He said: 'I do not know what al-khafqah and al-khafqatayn are.'
Indeed God Most High says: ﴿Nay, man is a witness against himself﴾ (al-Qiyamah 75:14).
Indeed 'Ali (AS) used to say: 'Whoever finds the taste of sleep, wudu is thereby made obligatory upon him.'

key_terms.الْخَفْقَةُ: a single nod/doze; juristic term for light sleep movement debated as a criterion for wudu invalidation
key_terms.الْوُضُوءُ: wudu (ritual ablution); made obligatory by truly experiencing sleep, not merely by outward appearance of nodding
key_terms.بَصِيرَةٌ: inner witness; Quranic term (75:14) indicating that each person possesses clear self-knowledge of their own state
key_terms.طَعْمَ النَّوْمِ: the 'taste' (experiential sensation) of sleep; the authoritative criterion established by Imam 'Ali (AS) for obligating wudu

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq (AS) say about whether nodding off (khafqah/khafqatayn) invalidates wudu, and what is the true criterion for sleep breaking ablution?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) dismisses the jurisprudential categories of al-khafqah (one nod) and al-khafqatayn (two nods) as criteria for invalidating wudu, redirecting the questioner from outward appearance to the Quranic principle that every person is their own inner witness (75:14). He then transmits the authoritative ruling of Imam 'Ali (AS): wudu is obligatory upon whoever truly experiences the 'taste of sleep,' regardless of how many head-nods were observed externally.
